lead: Optimizers do not invent a clever trick for each statement. They apply a small set of repeated sources: work that is repeated, work that is useless, work that is known in advance, and work that is too costly. Each source names one pattern in the intermediate code and one rewrite that removes it. Learn the eight sources and you can spot them in any program and check whether a compiler found them. These eight are the classical core that most optimizers contain; other transformations, such as inlining and loop unrolling, exist and build on them. They are the raw material for the loop work in 6.5.
prereq: You need: 6.2 and 6.3 for basic blocks and block DAGs, and the three-address code of Unit 4, Syntax-Directed Translation and Intermediate Code.

blocks.text: A source of optimization is a pattern plus a rewrite. Every source gets two labels, and exam questions ask for both.

A machine-independent source looks only at the intermediate code, so any target benefits. Constant folding, constant propagation, common subexpression elimination, copy propagation, dead-code elimination and algebraic simplification are machine-independent.

A machine-dependent source uses facts about the target. Strength reduction is the standard example: a multiply becomes a shift or an add only if that is cheaper on that machine. Register allocation and instruction selection are also machine-dependent.

A local optimization works inside one basic block, and the block DAG of 6.3 is enough to drive it. A global optimization needs facts that cross block boundaries, which come from data-flow analysis in 6.6.
Practical order inside a compiler: machine-independent local passes, then global passes, then machine-dependent work during code generation.

sections.h3: The eight sources, one by one

blocks.text: These eight cover what the syllabi call the principal sources. Each definition below is followed by one rewrite.

items: Common subexpression elimination (CSE): if the same expression is evaluated twice and no operand changes in between, evaluate it once. a = b + c; d = b + c becomes d = a.

Copy propagation: after e = d, replace later uses of e by d until e or d is redefined. For example f = e + 1 becomes f = d + 1, and you stop at the first redefinition of e or d. Note that e = d * 1 → e = d is algebraic simplification, not copy propagation.
Dead-code elimination: delete an assignment whose target is never read afterwards. If y is never used, y = 6 goes.
Constant folding: evaluate a constant expression at compile time. 2 * 3 becomes 6.
Constant propagation: put the known value of a variable in place of the variable. x = 6; y = x + 0 becomes y = 6 + 0.
Algebraic simplification: apply identities of the type. x + 0 becomes x, x * 1 becomes x, x - 0 becomes x.
Strength reduction: replace a costly operation by a cheap one. i * 2 becomes i + i.
Code motion: move an expression to a place where it runs fewer times, usually out of a loop. The loop-specific forms are in 6.5.

sections.h3: Safety: the results must not change

blocks.text: A transformation is function-preserving when the new code gives the same outputs and the same side effects as the old code for every input. Function-preserving and semantics-preserving mean the same thing; use either name.

items: List what each statement reads and writes.
For CSE, confirm that no operand was redefined between the two evaluations.
Keep every call, every input or output, and every assignment to a volatile name; they have effects beyond their result.
Check the type before an algebraic identity: x * 0 becoming 0 is false for floating point, where 0 * ∞ is not 0.
Recompute the block DAG before and after, and compare the surviving outputs.

blocks.text: The word optimization is loose. A compiler reduces cost by a heuristic; it rarely finds the true optimum, and it must stop after a bounded number of passes.

figure.caption: The worked example pass by pass: seven statements fall to four, ending as a = b + c; e = a; f = i + i; print(a, e, f). Notice that x = 6 and y = 6 are created by folding and propagation and then thrown away as dead code, so the print never sees them.

spec.title: Worked example: 7 → 4
spec.aria: A chain of the optimizations from the worked example, applied in order to a seven-statement block: constant folding makes x = 6, constant propagation makes y = 6, common subexpression elimination gives d = a, algebraic simplification gives e = d, copy propagation gives e = a, strength reduction gives f = i + i, dead code deletes x and y, and the final block has four statements.

examples.question:
A basic block contains seven statements:
1  x = 2 * 3
2  y = x + 0
3  a = b + c
4  d = b + c
5  e = d * 1
6  f = i * 2
7  print(a, e, f)
Apply constant folding, constant propagation, common subexpression elimination, copy propagation, algebraic simplification, strength reduction and dead-code elimination. Show the block after each pass and state how many statements remain.
steps: Constant folding: 2 * 3 is a constant expression, so statement 1 becomes x = 6.
Constant propagation: x holds 6, so y = x + 0 becomes y = 6 + 0.
Constant folding again: 6 + 0 is constant, so statement 2 becomes y = 6.
Common subexpression elimination: statements 3 and 4 both compute b + c, and neither b nor c is redefined between them. Replace statement 4 by d = a.
Algebraic simplification: d * 1 is d, so statement 5 becomes e = d.
Copy propagation: d is a copy of a, so every use of d becomes a use of a, giving e = a.
Strength reduction: i * 2 costs a multiply; i + i costs an add, so statement 6 becomes f = i + i.
Dead-code elimination: y is never read after statement 2, so delete y = 6. With y gone, x = 6 is never read, so delete x = 6. Nothing else is dead: a, e and f are printed.
Count the statements: the block started with 7 and now has a = b + c, e = a, f = i + i, print(a, e, f), that is 4.
Final block: a = b + c; e = a; f = i + i; print(a, e, f). Same printed values as the original block, so every step was function-preserving.
examples.answer: Final block: a = b + c; e = a; f = i + i; print(a, e, f). The constants folded are x = 6 and y = 6, both dead, and the block shrinks from 7 statements to 4.
examples.check:
x = 2 * 3
y = x + 0
print(x)
print(y)
start = 7
end = 4
print(start)
print(end)

traps: A repeated expression stops being a common subexpression if any variable inside it is reassigned between the two evaluations. Recheck the operands before you reuse.
Dead-code elimination must not delete calls, input or output, or assignments to volatile names, because their effect survives even when the result is unused.

Algebraic simplification is not always safe for floating point: x * 0 → 0 fails when x is NaN or infinity, and x + 0 → x fails at x = −0.0, because −0.0 + 0.0 gives +0.0. The compiler may apply these rewrites only when it knows the value is finite and its zero sign does not matter.
Constant propagation is unsafe if the variable is reassigned on a path between the definition and the use; a constant known in one block is not known everywhere until data-flow analysis proves it.
Function-preserving and semantics-preserving are the same property. An answer that lets an optimization change output on a defined program loses marks.

quiz.q: Name any three machine-independent sources of optimization.
quiz.a: Constant folding, common subexpression elimination and dead-code elimination (constant propagation, copy propagation and algebraic simplification are also correct).

quiz.q: Why is strength reduction called machine-dependent while dead-code elimination is machine-independent?
quiz.a: Strength reduction replaces an operation by a cheaper one on a particular target, so it needs the target's instruction costs and timings. Dead-code elimination only needs to know which results are never read, which is a property of the intermediate code alone.

quiz.q: For this block: a = 4; b = a * a; c = a * a; d = b + c; print(d), apply constant propagation with folding, common subexpression elimination, copy propagation and dead-code elimination. Give the final block and the value printed.
quiz.a: a = 4 is known, so b = 16 and c = 16 by folding. CSE gives c = b, and copy propagation turns d = b + c into d = b + b. Final block: b = 16; d = b + b; print(d). After the folding, a = 4 is dead, and c is dead after CSE. b is 16, so d = 32 and the printed value is 32.

quiz.q: A block has e = d * 1, then d = d + 1, then f = e. Can copy propagation replace f = e by f = d? Justify.
quiz.a: No. e holds the old value of d, and d was redefined after the copy. Replacing f = e by f = d would read the new value and change the result, so the transformation is not function-preserving.

quiz.q: Simplify z = (x * 1) + 0 by algebraic simplification and state when the second step is unsafe for floating point.
quiz.a: x * 1 gives x, then x + 0 gives x, so the statement becomes z = x. The first step is safe for floating point except that a signalling NaN is quieted. The second step fails at x = −0.0, because −0.0 + 0.0 gives +0.0, so the compiler may apply x + 0 → x only when it knows the sign of zero does not matter.

quiz.q: State the difference between constant folding and constant propagation with one example each.
quiz.a: Constant folding evaluates an expression whose operands are already constants, for example 2 * 3 becomes 6. Constant propagation replaces a variable by a constant value it is known to hold, for example y = x + 0 becomes y = 6 + 0 when x is known to be 6.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production compilers run these passes repeatedly until the code stops changing, and each pass in LLVM or GCC is named after one of these sources. Search for LLVM's instcombine, GVN and SCCP passes to see the industrial versions. Newer work goes further than pattern rewrites: superoptimizers search for the cheapest instruction sequence that computes the same values, and equality-saturation tools such as egg store many equivalent programs at once. MLIR applies the same sources at the level of whole tensor operations.
